newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore U.S.-dollar stocks in demand.
newsitem.headline: Singapore U.S.-dollar stocks in demand.

text.p: The fall of the Singapore dollar is fueling demand for U.S. dollar-denominated stocks on the local market that were previously shunned, analysts said at the weekend.

"U.S. dollar-denominated stocks are doing well but not the local-denominated ones which form the largest component in the market," Angus Armstrong, regional economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell told Reuters.
"If you are a foreign investor and uncertain about the exchange rate, you move out of the local currency into U.S.-denominations. It's a straight substitution," he said.
U.S. dollar-denominated stocks had not been in great demand because the local currency was so strong.

But on Friday, the Singapore dollar fell to a 30-month low of 1.4665 to the greenback as U.S. funds continued to buy the dollar. The Singapore dollar was trading around 1.4300 to the U.S. dollar in early July.

Currency dealers said the Singapore dollar was playing catch-up to the regional currencies like the Malaysian ringgit and the Indonesian rupiah, which weakened as devaluation fever hit Southeast Asia following the shock Thai baht float.

"The Sing dollar is weak, primarily because the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) is conspicuously absent in defending the currency, which means it is allowing it to fall to a more reasonable level to maintain our competitiveness," said Violet Soh, research manager at AMMB-Fraser Securities.

"Two years ago, nobody was interested in U.S.-dollar-denominated stocks, but the recent strength of the dollar around the region has pushed up interest in these stocks," said a dealer with a local securities firm.
Among the U.S. dollar-listed stocks which hit new highs on Friday were CM Telecom, toy maker Wah Shing International, home decor firm Roly and consumer electronics product distributor Thakral.
Analysts said the weaker Singapore dollar has given the Singapore stock market a temporary boost but that they were worried about too much regional currency volatility.

"It is cheaper now. But if the currency becomes weaker, it will be a dampening influence on equities because nobody is going to invest now thinking there are going to be currency losses," Armstrong said.
"When there are all these currency attacks, people get jittery. The so-called Asia miracle is dented, funds will avoid the region on the whole," Soh said.
Analysts remained confident about Singapore's equity market.
"The 'Sing' dollar has fallen on low inflation unlike other Asian countries. The temporary effect is actually positive for our exports," Soh said.
She said she was recommending a buy for Singapore equities on the back of strong fundamentals and attractive valuations, especially companies which have well-diversified earnings bases.
On whether Singapore's safe-haven reputation would lure foreign funds here amid regional instability, Armstrong said:
"Safe-haven status doesn't help with all this currency volatility. Only after they are stabilised. If investors think the currency is going down, they won't invest," he said.
